Charitably read, Savitch stands for memoisation and Urysohn for "collapsed, separated classes admit a simple readout". | [NOTE-475](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-475.md) | Deep Equals Shallow for ReLU Networks in Kernel Regimes | For κ(xᵀx′) on S^(d−1), µ_k = (ω_(d−2)/ω_(d−1)) ∫ κ(t)P_k(t)(1 − t²)^((d−3)/2) dt (Eq. 8), shared by N(d, k) ~ k^(d−2) harmonics. Theorem 1: an endpoint expansion κ(1 − t) = p(t) + c t^ν + o(t^ν) with ν non-integer gives µ_k ~ C k^(−d−2ν+1), parity-dependent. ReLU kernels have ν = 1/2 (NTK) and 3/2 (random features) at any depth, so the deep NTK decays as k^(−d) and the deep RF kernel as k^(−d−2) (Corollaries 2–3). MNIST and Fashion-MNIST accuracy is flat in depth from L = 2 to 5 (Table 1). | Read |
| [NOTE-476](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-476.md) v2 | Prevalence of Neural Collapse during the terminal phase of deep learning training | NC1 Σ_W → 0 (Tr(Σ_WΣ_B†)/C falls), NC2 centred means → simplex ETF (cosines → −1/(C−1)), NC3 W ∝ Ṁᵀ, NC4 nearest class mean; 7 datasets × 3 nets, 480 models. Median TPT gains: +0.35 points test accuracy, +0.0252 DeepFool robustness. NC1–2 ⇒ NC3–4 for Webb–Lowe and max-margin (Theorems 2, 4). Optimal small-noise error exponent C/(C−1)·1/4, only at simplex ETFs (Theorem 5). | Read |
| [NOTE-478](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-478.md) | The Full Spectrum of Deepnet Hessians at Scale | Hess = H + G (Gauss–Newton). At 28M parameters the Hessian has a bulk and about C outliers; outliers are in G, the bulk mostly in H; H is symmetric and power-law, φ ∝ \|λ\|⁻²·⁷ (R² 0.99), not Marchenko–Pastur or semicircle. G = A₁ + A₂ + B₁ + B₂ (Eq. 5): C class means give the outliers, cross-class spread and within-pair spread give two bulks. FastLanczos costs O(Mnp) time and O(p) memory. | Read |
| [NOTE-479](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-479.md) | Measurements of Three-Level Hierarchical Structure in the Outliers in the Spectrum of Deepnet Hessians | G = (1/n)ΔΔᵀ with δᵢ,c,c′ = column c′ of diag(√p)(I − 1pᵀ)∂f/∂θ. C² group means δc,c′, C cluster centres δc; G = G₀ + G₁ + G₂ + G₃ (Eq. 28). Top-C eigenvalues of G ≈ those of G₁ = (C−1)Ave_c δcδcᵀ, from a C×C Gram matrix, with λc(G) ≥ λc(G₁₊₂) ≥ λc(G₁). 18,000 CIFAR/MNIST models plus ImageNet VGG16/ResNet50. Group means switch from clustering by logit c′ to by class c during training. | Read |
| [NOTE-481](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-481.md) | The Convergence Rate of Neural Networks for Learned Functions of Different Frequencies | For uniform data the wide two-layer ReLU Gram matrix H∞ is a convolution on the sphere, so its eigenvectors are Fourier modes or spherical harmonics. On S¹, bias-free: λ_k = 1/π², 1/4, 2(k²+1)/(π²(k²−1)²) and 0 for k = 0, 1, even k ≥ 2 and odd k ≥ 3 (Eq. 12). With zero-initialised bias, odd k ≥ 3 get 1/(π²k²) (Eq. 13). Learning time grows as k² on S¹ and about k³ on S², as measured for shallow, deep and residual networks (Figs. 6–7). | Read |
| [NOTE-483](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-483.md) | Towards Understanding the Spectral Bias of Deep Learning | Theorem 4.2: n^(−1/2)‖V_(r_k)ᵀ(y − ŷ(T))‖ ≤ 2(1 − λ_(r_k))^T n^(−1/2)‖V_(r_k)ᵀy‖ + ε for any labels, given n ≥ Ω̃(ε^(−2) max{(λ_(r_k) − λ_(r_k+1))^(−2), M⁴r_k²}) and m ≥ Ω̃(poly(T, λ_(r_k)^(−1), ε^(−1))). Theorem 4.3: on uniform S^d the NTK's eigenfunctions are spherical harmonics, µ_k = 0 for odd k ≥ 3, and µ_k = Ω(max(k^(−d−1), d^(−k+1))) for even k. Experiments in R¹⁰ learn degrees 1, 2, 4 in that order, also on three non-uniform densities. | Read |
| [NOTE-516](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-516.md) | Taxonomizing local versus global structure in neural network loss landscapes | mc(θ, θ′) = ½(L(θ) + L(θ′)) − L(γ(t*)) on a trained Bezier curve, in 0-1 training error (Eq. 4); mc < 0 is a barrier, mc ≈ 0 well connected, mc > 0 unconverged ends. With Hessian top eigenvalue and trace and output CKA on mixup points, a load by temperature grid splits into phases I–IV, with IV-B (flat, connected, similar) the most accurate. Sharpness alone mispredicts across phases; with 10% label noise, the sharp phases beat flat but poorly connected phase III, and double descent appears along the Hessian transition. | Read |
| [NOTE-518](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-518.md) | Exact expressions for double descent and implicit regularization via surrogate random design | Surrogate design S^n_μ = Det(μ, K), density ∝ pdet(XXᵀ), K Poisson(γn) truncated at d. E[#rows] = n (Lemma 1); E[I − X̄⁺X̄] = (γnΣ + I)⁻¹ (Lemma 2); E[tr((X̄ᵀX̄)⁺)] = γn(1 − det((I/γn + Σ)⁻¹Σ)) (Lemma 3); λn = 1/γn. These give exact MSE in all regimes (Theorem 1) and E[X̄⁺ȳ] = (Σ + λnI)⁻¹v for n < d, with n = tr(Σ(Σ + λnI)⁻¹) (Theorem 2). For sub-Gaussian rows the i.i.d.-design MSE converges to the surrogate formula (Theorem 3), at an observed O(1/d) rate. | Read |
| [NOTE-519](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-519.md) | A Random Matrix Analysis of Random Fourier Features: Beyond the Gaussian Kernel, a Precise Phase Transition, and the Corresponding Double Descent | Q̄ = ((N/n)(Kcos/(1+δcos) + Ksin/(1+δsin)) + λI)⁻¹ with δσ = (1/n) tr KσQ̄ is a deterministic equivalent for E_W[(ΣXᵀΣX/n + λI)⁻¹] (Theorem 1); Ē_train and Ē_test follow (Theorems 2–3). As λ → 0, δ ~ 1/λ for 2N < n and O(1) for 2N > n; det(Ω⁻¹) ~ λ, so Ē_test → ∞ at 2N = n unless the test set is within σ² ≲ λ of the training set. N/n → ∞ recovers Gaussian kernel regression. Theory matches MNIST, Fashion- and Kannada-MNIST. | Read |
| [NOTE-525](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-525.md) | Does Data Scaling Lead to Visual Compositional Generalization? | (n, k) framework: two concepts with n values, k seen combinations per value. From-scratch ResNet-50s: near-100% ID, large OOD drops; 4× ID data leaves 60–80% drops; more values or combinations help. Features go from spurious, to decodable but entangled, to linearly factored (R² > 0.8, cosine < 0.1–0.2). Proposition 4.1: with linearly factored embeddings spanning 2n − 1 dimensions, k = 2 suffices for a linear classifier to be correct on all (n − k)·n unseen pairs. DINO, DINOv2, CLIP: partly factored, above chance, not perfect. | Read |
| [NOTE-529](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-529.md) | Unveiling Mode Connectivity in Graph Neural Networks | GCN node-classification solutions from different seeds show linear loss barriers that vary by graph (small on Cora, Citeseer; large on Coauthor-CS, Squirrel) and vanish along fitted quadratic Bezier curves. GCN, GraphSAGE and GAT give similar barriers, MLPs different ones. On CSBM graphs barriers fall with density and feature separability and peak at middling homophily. Stated without proof: a barrier bound through the spectral gap, a generalisation bound proportional to the barrier, and a Wasserstein distance between graphs' interpolation-loss curves that bounds the domain-adaptation gap. | Read |
| [NOTE-536](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-536.md) | The Generalization Ridge: Information Flow in Natural Language Generation | I(Zℓ; Y) = H(G_Z) + H(G_Y) − H(G_Z ∘ G_Y), with H(G) = −tr(G log G) on trace-normalized Gaussian Gram matrices (bandwidth 1) of ℓ2-normalized last-token states and target-token embeddings. It rises, peaks at layers 10/12 (GPT-2-S, synthetic: 0.2721) and falls (0.0188 at layer 12), where OOD early-exit accuracy peaks (56.90%) and ID accuracy keeps rising (93.17%). Middle residual updates add most; OOD-fitted residual scales downweight the last layers. The profile's shape persists over 50 decoding steps. | Read |
| [NOTE-541](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-541.md) | Intermediate Layer Classifiers for OOD generalization | ILC_l(x) = W_l r_l(x) + b_l on frozen layer-l features, l ≤ L − 2, layer chosen on OOD validation data. Few-shot, best ILC minus last-layer retraining: +16.8, +6.3, +1.6, +6.3 points (ResNets on CMNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100C, MultiCelebA); +27.0 on MultiCelebA at π ≤ 0.03. Zero-shot worst-group accuracy: Waterbirds 79.4 → 87.1, CelebA 56.0 → 82.0, MultiCelebA 20.8 → 46.0. Layer 7 beats 8 everywhere in Figure 8. Intermediate features are less displaced by shift for minority groups. | Read |
| [NOTE-542](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-542.md) | Rethinking generalization requires revisiting old ideas: statistical mechanics approaches and complex learning behavior | VSDL model: f = f(x; α, τ), α = m_eff/N lowered by label noise, τ raised by early stopping. Thermodynamic limit m, N → ∞ with α = m/N fixed. Continuous perceptron: s(ε) ~ ln ε, so 1/ε − α = 0 gives ε ~ 1/α (Eqs. 6–8). Ising perceptron: s(ε) ~ −(π²/2)ε² ln ε, and −π²ε ln ε = α has no solution for large α, so ε falls discontinuously to 0 at αc (Eqs. 9–13). Rigorous bound: error ≤ ε* + ε_τ, ε* the rightmost crossing of s(ε) and −α log(1 − ε) (Eqs. 14–18). No new theorem, no experiment. | Read |
| [NOTE-544](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-544.md) | Explaining Landscape Connectivity of Low-cost Solutions for Multilayer Nets | ε-dropout-stable ReLU nets are ε-connected by a piecewise-linear path (Theorem 1); ε-noise-stable nets by 10 segments with barrier Õ(ε) (Theorem 2), or 13 through a narrow low-loss net (Theorem 3). For any width there is a teacher dataset on which a two-layer student's global minima are disconnected (Theorem 4). MNIST convnets and a VGG-11 on CIFAR-10 satisfy the conditions roughly. | Read |
| [NOTE-620](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-620.md) | Learning to (Learn at Test Time) | Recasts a sequence-modelling layer as a learner trained on the sequence it reads: hidden state as inner-model weights, update as a gradient step on a learned self-supervised loss. | [NOTE-621](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-621.md) | Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent | Constructs weights for which one linear self-attention layer reproduces, on every token, the data change induced by one gradient step of a linear model on the in-context regression loss, so the query's output equals the post-update prediction; shows a trained single layer finds these weights up to scale, and that deeper trained models implement a curvature-corrected variant (GD++) rather than gradient descent. | Read |
| [NOTE-633](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-633.md) | Implicit Bayesian inference account of in-context learning | Proves that if pretraining text is a mixture of HMMs and a model fits it exactly, conditioning on a prompt of concatenated examples recovers the prompt's latent concept by posterior concentration, and the in-context predictor is asymptotically Bayes-optimal, whenever each example's KL signal about the concept beats the error from the improbable transitions between examples. The account is of the data distribution, not of any network's computation. | Read |
| [NOTE-637](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-637.md) | Test-Time Training for Few-Shot Learning | Shows that turning a task's few-shot demonstrations into a temporary weight update (per-task LoRA on leave-one-out in-context tasks) improves an 8B model over conditioning on the same demonstrations: 50.5% → 57.8% on BIG-Bench Hard, and large gains on ARC. The update works best when it is trained in the in-context format, and gains concentrate on tasks with structural rules or distribution shift. | Read |
| [NOTE-658](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-658.md) v2 | Exact Learning Dynamics of In-Context Learning in Linear Transformers | Solves the averaged gradient-flow dynamics of one linear-attention layer trained on in-context regression, when tasks and input covariance share an eigenbasis and the weights are assumed to stay in it: each mode is a logistic curve on timescale (ηP s_α²)⁻¹, so learning is staged by the input spectrum, and the fixed point is the known preconditioned predictor W Σ̂_x [((N+1)/N)Σ_x + (Tr Σ_x/N)I]⁻¹. A scaling symmetry conserves ‖p₂‖² − ‖q₁‖². The transfer to non-linear transformers and grokking is a set of timing coincidences in spectral measures. | Read |
| [NOTE-660](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-660.md) | Closed-Form Training Dynamics in Word2Vec-like Models | Proves that word2vec's loss, approximated to fourth order and reweighted so that every pair carries the same aggregate weight, is unweighted factorisation of M*, the relative deviation of co-occurrence from independence, whose rank-d minimisers are its top eigenvectors; derives, without full rigour, that gradient flow from small random initialisation learns those eigenvectors one at a time in sigmoidal steps; and shows on Wikipedia that the predicted embeddings match word2vec's features and scores better than truncated PMI or PPMI. Its account of analogies is an empirical spiked-random-matrix fit. | Read |
| [NOTE-661](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-661.md) | Single-Head Attention in High Dimensions | In a solvable model, one tied softmax attention layer trained by ridge-penalized ERM on Gaussian sequences with n ∝ d² samples, derives (non-rigorously, by AMP and random-matrix theory) the test error, interpolation and recovery thresholds, and the spectrum of the learned query–key map, η·ReLU(S0 + δZ − ε): outliers are recovered target directions, the bulk is finite-sample noise, and weight decay acts as a nuclear norm. Power-law targets are recovered mode by mode, giving heavy-tailed spectra and LASSO-rate scaling laws. | Read |
| [NOTE-662](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-662.md) | Towards Understanding Grokking | In a model that decodes the sum of two learned embeddings, a held-out pair is answered correctly when its embedding sum coincides with a trained pair's, and the training set's same-answer pairs force such coincidences. Grokking's critical training fraction is then where those equations first fix the embedding up to translation and scale, which a posited effective loss predicts for addition with p = 10. Threshold-defined phase diagrams over decoder learning rate and weight decay put grokking between comprehension and memorization, in the toy and, qualitatively, in a transformer and on MNIST. | Read |
| [NOTE-666](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-666.md) | A mathematical theory of semantic development in deep neural networks | Shows that a two-layer linear network trained from small weights learns the singular modes of its input–output correlations in order of strength, each by a sharp sigmoidal transition, where a shallow network learns all modes together; and that the singular structure of data generated on trees, rings and clusters, plus a minimum-norm property, accounts for coarse-to-fine differentiation, transient errors, narrowing generalisation, typicality, coherence thresholds and conserved representational similarity. Exact only from decoupled, balanced initial weights with white inputs; random initialisation is simulated. | Read |
| [NOTE-667](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-667.md) | Exact solutions to the nonlinear dynamics of learning in deep linear neural networks | Derives the coupled gradient-descent equations of a linear network with hidden layers and whitened inputs, and solves them exactly from decoupled starts: one sigmoid per singular mode of the input–output correlation, with conserved differences of squared layer strengths; balanced or not with one hidden layer, from equal layer strengths at any depth. Depth slows learning only through the initial end-to-end mode strength, so from strength of order one the iteration count stays finite as depth grows when the step size is scaled down with depth. Argues, with MNIST and random-matrix simulations, that orthogonal layers or suitable pretraining give such starts and scaled Gaussian layers do not, and that orthogonal tanh networks near gain 1 keep their Jacobians near-isometric. | Read |
| [NOTE-677](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-677.md) | The Random Hierarchy Model | Introduces the Random Hierarchy Model, a random context-free grammar in which each symbol has m synonymic expansions, and shows by experiment that deep feature-learning networks learn it from about n_c m^L examples, polynomial in the input dimension, while shallow and lazy networks need an exponential number. That size coincides with the emergence of synonym-invariant hidden representations and, by a scaling argument, with the size at which the class statistics of input patches, equal for synonyms, exceed sampling noise; removing those statistics makes deep networks fail as well. | Read |
| [NOTE-684](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-684.md) | The Sparse Random Hierarchy Model | Adds sparsity to the Random Hierarchy Model, so that labels are unchanged by discrete displacements of the informative features, and shows by experiment that deep networks learn it from a number of examples polynomial in the input dimension, (s0 + 1)^L n_c m^L up to a factor s^(L/2) without weight sharing and (s0 + 1)^2 n_c m^L with it, and that hidden layers become insensitive to synonym swaps and to feature displacements at about the same training-set size as test error falls. That coincidence is offered as the reason deformation stability tracks performance on images, which is not tested on images. | Read |
| [NOTE-687](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-687.md) | How the structure of language is acquired | Extends the Random Hierarchy Model to predicting a masked last token. The correlation between two tokens shrinks by about a factor m per level of their common ancestor, a sample of P sequences resolves it only above a (v²P)^(−1/2) noise floor, and deep transformers and CNNs show loss steps at P_ℓ ≈ v m^(2ℓ−1), where their layers come to encode the level-ℓ hidden symbol. On character-level text, the correlation decay exponent predicts where the loss for a given context length levels off. The route from correlations to learned hidden variables is argued, not proved. | Read |
| [NOTE-688](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-688.md) v2 | Why does deep and cheap learning work so well? | Argues that cheap networks suffice because physical data have low-order, local, symmetric Hamiltonians, and that depth pays because inference must compose the sufficient statistics of a Markov generative hierarchy; proves that one hidden layer needs exactly 2^n neurons to multiply n inputs. On renormalization it is right that a coarse-graining needs a stated target, and its early appendix shows that neither a matched partition function nor the exact trace condition supplies one; it is wrong that the target must come from supervision. | Read |
| [NOTE-689](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-689.md) | Deriving neural scaling laws from language statistics | Predicts the data-limited scaling exponent of language-model test loss as γ/(2β), from two measured corpus statistics: the decay with lag of the top singular value of the token–token covariance (β), which sets the usable context n*(P) ~ P^(1/(2β)), and the decay of next-token conditional entropy with context (γ). The derivation rests on assumed scaling forms and a fast-learning condition; on TinyStories and WikiText-103 transformers match the predicted exponents up to about 10^8 tokens and horizons of a few tens of tokens. | Read |
| [NOTE-693](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-693.md) | The power of deeper networks for expressing natural functions | Proves that a single hidden layer of smooth, bias-free units needs exactly ∏(rᵢ+1) neurons to Taylor-approximate x₁^r₁⋯xₙ^rₙ while a deep network needs O(Σ log rᵢ), extends the gap to sparse and univariate polynomials, and bounds a product of n inputs at depth k by about 2^(n^(1/k)). Its uniform-approximation lower bounds rest on an unproved step, the depth-k tightness is a conjecture, and the gap is set by degree, so bounded-degree polynomials show none. | Read |
| [NOTE-711](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-711.md) | The Limiting Dynamics of SGD | SGD with momentum β, learning rate η, batch size S and weight decay λ is modelled as (η/2)(1 + β)θ̈ + (1 − β)θ̇ + λθ = −g(θ) + √(η/S) √Σ ξ(t). For linear regression with Σ = σ²H this is an OU process in phase space. Its stationary state is Gibbs on a modified loss, with inverse temperature κ = S(1 − β²), in broken detailed balance. Under a quadratic loss at the end of training the same holds for deep networks, and a ResNet-18 on ImageNet shows the predicted isotropy, velocity regularization, oscillations and speed. | Read |
| [NOTE-712](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-712.md) | Symmetry in Neural Network Parameter Spaces | A symmetry is a group action on parameters preserving the network function (Def. 2.4) or the loss (Def. 2.6), possibly only on given data or in expectation (Defs. 2.8–2.9). Common components have GL, scaling, sign-flip, orthogonal, translation and permutation symmetries (Table 1). Continuous symmetries make minima connected manifolds, and give gradient flow conserved quantities that label trajectories and endpoints (§5). SGD's finite steps, noise and weight decay break these, which is an open route to implicit bias (§7.2). | Read |
| [NOTE-713](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-713.md) | Neural Mechanics | A symmetry ψ of the loss gives ⟨∇L, ∂_α ψ⟩ = 0 and a Hessian constraint. Under gradient flow, Theorem 1 conserves ⟨θ, ∂_α ψ⟩: for translation ⟨θ_A, 1⟩, for scale \|θ_A\|², for rescale \|θ_A1\|² − \|θ_A2\|². With weight decay λ and the modified loss L + (η/4)\|∇L\|², these become exponentially decaying memories plus integrals of gradient norms (Eqs. 18–20), matched on VGG-16 with Tiny ImageNet. The noise covariance annihilates the generators (§5, App. F). | Read |
| [NOTE-714](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-714.md) | Noise Balance and Stationary Distribution of Stochastic Gradient Descent | SDE: dθ = −∇L dt + √(T C(θ)) dW, with T = η/S. With ℓ(u, w) = ℓ(λu, w/λ), d(‖u‖² − ‖w‖²)/dt = −T(uᵀC₁u − wᵀC₂w) (Theorem 1). The stationary point is Tr C(w) = Tr C(u). With weight decay γ the rate is TC₀ + γ (Corollary 2.1). Diagonal linear network ℓ = (Σᵢ ∏ₖ u_i^{(k)} x − y)²: sign coherence and balance for depth D > 1 (Theorem 3), exact stationary distribution (Theorem 4), collapse above T_c = β₂/α₃ for D = 1, tail ∝ v^{−5+3/(D+1)} independent of data. | Read |
| [NOTE-715](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-715.md) | From Lazy to Rich: Exact Learning Dynamics in Deep Linear Networks | Two-layer linear network ŷ = W₂W₁x, MSE, full-batch gradient flow. Assumptions: whitened inputs (A1), λ-balanced start W₂ᵀW₂ − W₁W₁ᵀ = λI (A2), no bottleneck (A3). Then QQᵀ, with Q = [W₁ᵀ; W₂], obeys a matrix Riccati equation (Lemma 4.1), solved exactly (Theorem 4.3). For aligned starts, each singular value moves by a λ-dependent transition function: sigmoidal as λ → 0, exponential 1 − e^{−\|λ\|t/τ} as \|λ\| → ∞ (Theorem 5.1). | Read |
| [NOTE-716](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-716.md) | Symmetry Induces Structure and Constraint of Learning | ℓ_γ = ℓ₀(θ, x) + γ‖θ‖². O-mirror symmetry: ℓ₀(θ) = ℓ₀((I − 2OOᵀ)θ). Theorem 1: (1) Oᵀθ = 0 implies Oᵀ∇ℓ_γ = 0; (2) at symmetric points the Hessian splits into ker(Oᵀ) and im(OOᵀ) blocks; (3) above some γ₀ the projection (I − OOᵀ)θ has lower loss; (4) above some γ₁ all minima satisfy Oᵀθ = 0. SGD near the symmetric set: Pθ_{t+1} = Pθ_t − λH(x)Pθ_t, attractive when the Lyapunov exponent E log\|1 − λ(ξ + γ)\| < 0. Corollaries: sparsity, low rank, homogeneous neurons (Theorems 2–4). | Read |
| [NOTE-738](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-738.md) | Nielsen et al. — When Does Closeness in Distribution Imply Representational Similarity? | For softmax models p(y\|x) ∝ exp(f(x)ᵀg(y)), equal distributions fix the embeddings up to an invertible linear map, but KL closeness does not: by making the unembedding norm large, two models' KL divergence goes to zero while their embeddings stay fixed and are not linearly related. A log-likelihood variance distance does bound a representational dissimilarity, d_LLV ≤ ε ⇒ d_f,g ≤ 2Mε. Whether closeness in distribution implies similar representations depends on which distance is used. | Read |
| [NOTE-740](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-740.md) v2 | HaoChen et al. — Spectral Contrastive Loss | On a finite augmentation space, the spectral contrastive loss L(f) = −2E[f(x)ᵀf(x⁺)] + E[(f(x)ᵀf(x⁻))²] equals the rank-k factorization loss ‖D^(−1/2)AD^(−1/2) − FFᵀ‖²_F up to a constant when the rows of F are w_x^(1/2) f(x), so its minimizers are the top-k eigenvectors of the normalized augmentation graph up to row scaling and a right rotation. A linear probe on them has error Õ(α/ρ²_⌊k/2⌋), where α is the label noise of augmentations and ρ the sparsest-partition conductance. | Read |
| [NOTE-741](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-741.md) | Simon et al. — On the Stepwise Nature of Self-Supervised Learning | For a simplified Barlow Twins loss on a linear or kernel model trained by gradient flow from small initialization, the embedding learns the top eigenvectors of a symmetrized cross-correlation operator one at a time, each at a time set by its eigenvalue, and lands on the minimum-norm zero-loss solution: kernel PCA on K_Γ. Exact for aligned initialization; an informal derivation for generic small initialization. ResNets trained with Barlow Twins, SimCLR and VICReg show the same stepwise rank growth, which is an empirical finding, not a consequence of the theory. | Read |
| [NOTE-742](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-742.md) | Sefidgaran, Zaidi & Krasnowski — MDL and Generalization Guarantees for Representation Learning | The expected generalisation error of an encoder–decoder classifier is bounded by 2√((2·MDL + K + 2)/n) + ε, where MDL is a KL divergence between the encoder's joint law of train-and-ghost latents and a prior symmetric under label-preserving permutations. The bound holds for any decoder, stays finite for deterministic continuous encoders under lossy compression, and is never evaluated numerically. A VIB variant with label-dependent learned priors gains about 2.5 points on CIFAR-10. | Read |
| [NOTE-751](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-751.md) v2 | Johnson, El Hanchi & Maddison — Contrastive Learning Can Find an Optimal Basis | On a finite augmentation space, the NT-Logistic and spectral losses are minimized over unconstrained kernels by K⁺ = p⁺/(p⊗p), and InfoNCE by K⁺ up to a factor constant on communicating classes. Kernel PCA under K⁺ returns the eigenfunctions of the positive-pair Markov chain (h_i = λ_i^(1/2) f_i). The top-d eigenfunctions span the subspace that minimizes worst-case L²(p) approximation error over targets with E_p⁺[(g(a₁) − g(a₂))²] ≤ ε; that error is ε/(2(1 − λ_(d+1))). | Read |
| [NOTE-754](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-754.md) | Fischer — The Conditional Entropy Bottleneck | The MNI criterion asks for I(X;Y) = I(X;Z) = I(Y;Z), and CEB targets it by minimizing I(X;Z\|Y) − γI(Y;Z), which is IB with γ = β − 1. CEB beats VIB at every ρ on Fashion MNIST for accuracy and robustness, and a CEB Wide ResNet beats Madry's adversarially trained model on CIFAR-10 without adversarial training. That retained information causes the robustness failures is a hypothesis, supported only by these experiments. | Read |
| [NOTE-760](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-760.md) | Grünwald & Roos — Minimum Description Length Revisited | A review of MDL since 2007. Each model is replaced by one universal distribution, chosen for small worst-case log-loss regret against the model's best fit. NML is the minimax choice, with complexity (k/2) log(n/2π) + log ∫ v√\|I\| + o(1). Estimation is penalised ML with a luckiness function v. The switch distribution nearly resolves AIC–BIC, the RIPr gives tests safe under optional continuation, and MDL and Bayes can be inconsistent under misspecification. Results are cited, not proved. | Read |
| [NOTE-762](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-762.md) | Kornblith, Chen, Lee & Norouzi — Why Do Better Loss Functions Lead to Less Transferable Features? | For ResNet-50 on ImageNet, every training objective that raises accuracy over softmax cross-entropy also raises penultimate-layer class separation, and fixed penultimate features with more class separation transfer worse to new-class datasets (Spearman ρ = −0.93 across nine objectives; one temperature knob moves both). The losses differ only in the last few blocks, and full fine-tuning erases the difference. For the pretraining classes themselves, more separation helps. | Read |
| [NOTE-764](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-764.md) | Thrampoulidis et al. — Imbalance Trouble | In the unconstrained-features model with cross-entropy and vanishing regularization, the max-margin solutions have logits exactly equal to the simplex-encoded label matrix Ẑ (one-hot minus 1/k), whatever the class imbalance. The classifier and embedding Gram matrices are VΛVᵀ and UΛUᵀ from Ẑ's SVD. This SELI geometry is the simplex ETF only for balanced or binary data. Under imbalance, majority classifiers are longer and minority classifiers closer together. No finite weight decay gives SELI, and SGD approaches it more slowly as imbalance grows. | Read |
| [NOTE-770](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-770.md) v2 | Zhai — Contextures: The Mechanism of Representation Learning | For any joint law of an input X and a context A, symmetric or not, the conditional-expectation operator from L²(P_A) to L²(P_X) has a singular value decomposition (assuming Hilbert–Schmidt), and its top-d left singular functions are a d-dimensional encoder (not the unique one, as the thesis says; see version 2) that minimizes worst-case linear-probe approximation error over tasks of compatibility at least 1−ε. Several squared-error objectives reach that span at their optimum. The claims about scaling and about moderate association are argued and measured, not proved. | Read |
| [NOTE-772](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-772.md) v2 | Kothapalli — Neural Collapse: A Review on Modelling Principles and Generalization | A survey, not a source of results. It sorts accounts of neural collapse into unconstrained-features models (the last-layer features are free variables) and local elasticity, and reports that every one of them derives the collapsed state or its dynamics only after removing the data. On generalization it finds the literature in conflict. Collapse on the training set does not guarantee good test error, test-set collapse is much weaker and dataset-dependent, and there is no agreed threshold for calling a network collapsed. It also reports that networks more collapsed on ImageNet transfer worse. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-774](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-774.md) | Kothapalli & Tirer — Can Kernel Methods Explain How the Data Affects Neural Collapse? | NC1, measured as tr Σ_W / tr Σ_B, is written for any kernel as a function of the kernel matrix. For two-class, one-dimensional Gaussian data with the classes on opposite sides of the origin, the ReLU NTK of a wide two-layer net is a scaled copy of the NNGP kernel within each class and zero across classes. So lazy-regime training leaves expected NC1 where it was at initialization. In higher dimensions the NTK is measured no more collapsed, and with ReLU less. A data-aware kernel lowers NC1 for separable data but tracks finite networks poorly when the classes overlap or are imbalanced. Erf collapses more than ReLU. | Read |
| [NOTE-776](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-776.md) | Grünwald & Vitányi — Shannon information and Kolmogorov complexity | A survey pairing Shannon's and Kolmogorov's notions. Expected Kolmogorov complexity exceeds entropy by between 0 and K(f) + O(1), and expected algorithmic mutual information lies between I(X;Y) − K(f) and I(X;Y) + 2K(f). An algorithmic sufficient statistic is probabilistically nearly sufficient in expectation, one way only. The expected structure function brackets the distortion-rate function with a K(f, d, m, R) shift in rate. Each link holds only up to the complexity of the distribution. | Read |
| [NOTE-777](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-777.md) | Belrose et al. — Neural Networks Learn Statistics of Increasing Complexity | An empirical paper. Vision networks trained on real images classify maximum-entropy samples that match only the class means, or means and covariances, well above chance early in training (peaks between about 2^4 and 2^12 steps), and the accuracy then falls, often below chance. First-order samples peak earlier and lower than second-order ones. Pythia models fit unigram-sampled text, then bigram-sampled text, then fit them worse, then better again. The n-gram/moment equivalence is an identity of one-hot indicators. The ordering argument is a heuristic. | Read |
| [NOTE-780](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-780.md) | Sefidgaran, Gohari, Richard & Şimşekli — Rate-Distortion Theoretic Generalization Bounds | The expected generalisation error of any algorithm is at most √(2σ²·R/n) + ε, where R is the least mutual information I(S;Ŵ) of any surrogate output whose expected generalisation error is within ε. With ε = 0 this is Xu–Raginsky. With ε > 0 it stays finite where I(S;W) is infinite. For a Lipschitz loss R becomes the rate-distortion function of the output's marginal law, and as ε → 0 its rate-distortion dimension. A tail bound replaces I(S;W) by its supremum over laws within log(1/δ) in KL. Every bound depends on the unknown data distribution. | Read |
| [NOTE-783](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-783.md) | Han, Papyan & Donoho — Neural Collapse Under MSE Loss | Networks trained with MSE loss show neural collapse on five datasets and three architectures. The MSE loss splits exactly into a term for the least-squares classifier of the current features and a non-negative deviation term, and the deviation becomes negligible early in training. On that "central path", in an unconstrained-features model with no weight decay and features continually renormalized to identity within-class covariance, gradient flow drives every singular value of Σ_W^(−1/2)M̃ to infinity as (4t/N)^(1/4), and drives them to equality. That gives NC1–NC4 in closed form. | Read |
| [NOTE-787](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-787.md) v2 | Vereshchagin & Vitányi — Kolmogorov's structure functions and model selection | For a string x of length n and every complexity bound α, the minimal two-part code length λ_x(α), the structure function h_x(α) + α and the best achievable fit β_x(α) + K(x) are one function to within O(log n), and any set witnessing λ_x or h_x also witnesses β_x. Every non-increasing shape occurs for some x. h_x and λ_x are upper semicomputable but not computable; β_x is not even semicomputable. Finite sets only; the extension to computable distributions costs O(log n). | Read |
| [NOTE-790](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-790.md) | Vitányi — Meaningful Information | With total recursive functions as models, the shortest model that completes an optimal two-part code for a string (its sophistication) is a non-trivial split of its information into structure and noise. With partial recursive models the split collapses to zero for every string. The total-function, computable-distribution and finite-set classes agree to within logarithmic terms. Some strings of every length are almost all structure, and sophistication is not computable. | Read |
| [NOTE-794](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-794.md) | Liu et al. — Physics of Skill Learning | Three toy models of skill learning. In the Geometry model, independent skills are orthogonal directions in parameter space weighted by frequency. Under SGD each is learned at its own rate, the second taking about 1/p₂ as long. Under sign descent they compete for coordinate signs, and each starts as the one before finishes (the Domino effect), so the n-th skill takes time ∝ n. A one-parameter Resource ODE fits these curves and has exact conserved quantities u_i^(1/p_i). A small MLP also shows the effect when one parity is the XOR of two others. | Read |
| [NOTE-796](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-796.md) | Gu et al. — Data Mixing Can Induce Phase Transitions in Knowledge Acquisition | An optimal capacity-bounded learner, given a mixture of equally frequent random facts and a second domain, learns none of the facts until the second domain's marginal loss reduction per unit of capacity falls below r·p/(1−r), then all of them within Htot more capacity. Pythia models trained on synthetic biographies mixed into web text show near-zero recall below a threshold model size and mixing ratio, and 4–16 times more training barely moves it. | Read |
| [NOTE-800](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-800.md) | Noroozizadeh et al. — Deep sequence models tend to memorize geometrically | Transformers and Mamba trained only on a graph's edge bigrams embed nodes so that multi-hop relations are readable, and solve an in-weights path-finding task built to defeat next-token learning. The authors argue that supervision, capacity, ease of optimization and succinctness each fail to explain why this geometry wins over an associative lookup. In a wide two-layer weight-tied model under unregularized cross-entropy the embeddings settle into the top Laplacian eigenvectors without a rank bottleneck, shown empirically, with an informal partial proof. Why deeper models prefer geometry is left open. | Read |
| [NOTE-801](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-801.md) | Vitányi & Li — MDL induction, Bayesianism and Kolmogorov complexity | With the universal prior, the Fundamental Inequality puts −log Pr(D\|H) − log P(H) within α = K(Pr(·\|H)) + K(P) of K(D\|H) + K(H) when D is random for H and H is random for P. So ideal MDL and MAP agree to a factor 2^{−α} among such "admissible" hypotheses. α can be as large as K(H), and outside the admissible set the two can pick different hypotheses. For finite-set models, MAP, ideal MDL and Kolmogorov's minimal sufficient statistic coincide. | Read |
| [NOTE-804](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-804.md) | Goldwasser et al. — A Theory of Unsupervised Translation Motivated by Animal Communication | With a plausibility prior over the target language and no parallel data, maximum likelihood learns a translator whose error is bounded like a supervised Occam bound divided by the common ground. In the common-nonsense model err = O(log\|Θ\| / (α·min(m,\|T\|))), tight up to a constant; in the knowledge-graph model more knowledge per node needs less agreement. Information-theoretic only, lossless, uniform languages. | Read |
| [NOTE-805](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-805.md) | Defilippis et al. — Optimal scaling laws in learning hierarchical multi-index models | For Gaussian inputs, n = αd samples, and a target Σ_k a_k g_k(⟨w_k, x⟩) with even links and a_k ~ k^(−γ), direction k becomes weakly recoverable at α_k = Θ(a_k^(−2)) = Θ(k^(2γ)) for γ > 1/2. The Bayes-optimal weighted subspace error is Θ(α^(−1+1/(2γ))) before α ≍ m⋆^(2γ) and Θ(m⋆/α) after. A target-agnostic spectral estimator attains both, and a two-layer net given that estimator as its first layer, with a ridge readout, attains them in excess risk. The cascade is in sample size. The link to gradient descent is a remark. | Read |
| [NOTE-806](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-806.md) | Sefidgaran & Zaidi — Data-Dependent Generalization Bounds via Variable-Size Compressibility | If the number of codewords allowed for covering a block of experiments may depend on the realised sample and output, generalisation bounds can be data-dependent. The general bounds are change-of-measure inequalities that cover tail, PAC-Bayes and in-expectation forms. With the rate set to log dP_{W\|S}/dP(W) for a fixed prior P, the tail bound is the disintegrated PAC-Bayes bound. A new trajectory bound is data-dependent except for a coupling term, and its experiment drops that term. | Read |
| [NOTE-807](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-807.md) | Gokhale — The semantic landscape paradigm for neural networks | A conceptual proposal with no experiment and no proof. Training is pictured as a walk on a graph of "heuristic models" (internal algorithms), ranked by a fallibility F. A critical dataset size for grokking and emergence with scale are each argued to be graph connectivity thresholds, and power-law scaling in time, data and size is derived from an assumed trap model of activated hops. The percolation is asserted, not shown, and the scaling laws rest on chosen assumptions. | Read |
| [NOTE-815](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-815.md) | Gerstgrasser et al. — Is Model Collapse Inevitable? | In a fixed-design linear regression refit each round to labels drawn from the previous fit, keeping every earlier round's data gives test error σ²d/(T−d−1)·Σ1/i², bounded by π²/6 times the first fit's, where replacing the data gives σ²d/(T−d−1)·n. The error still rises every round. Small language models and a diffusion model on accumulated data hold their test loss over five to eight rounds; a VAE's still rises, more slowly. | Read |
| [NOTE-833](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-833.md) | Sun, Shi, Liang & Li — when known classes help discover novel ones | In a spectral-contrastive augmentation graph over labelled and unlabelled data, the linear-probe residual of a novel labelling is exactly the part of it outside the top-k eigenspace that the labelled rows of the discarded eigenvectors cannot absorb. Known classes that share the novel class's attribute can make it zero, and a toy shows that known classes sharing a rival attribute make it worse. The general error bound (Theorem 5.6) is approximate and averages all known classes into one block. | Read |
| [NOTE-836](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-836.md) | Schölkopf, Herbrich & Smola — A Generalized Representer Theorem | For any nonempty set X, real positive-definite kernel k, strictly increasing g and any cost c on the training triples, even coupled, non-convex or infinite-valued, every minimizer of c + g(‖f‖) over the class F of countable kernel expansions with finite RKHS norm is a finite expansion Σ α_i k(·, x_i) at the training points. The proof uses only the reproducing property and Pythagoras. Existence of a minimizer, the extension from F to the completed RKHS, and the semiparametric Theorem 2 are not proved here. | Read |
| [NOTE-838](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-838.md) | Muandet et al. — Kernel Mean Embedding of Distributions | A survey whose load-bearing chain is short and explicit. An RKHS is a Hilbert space with bounded evaluation, so Riesz gives k_x (Thm 2.4, Prop. 2.1). If E_P√k(X,X) < ∞, the expectation functional is bounded and Riesz gives μ_P with E_P f = ⟨f, μ_P⟩ (Lemma 3.1, proved). MMD is ‖μ_P − μ_Q‖ (eq. 3.29), a metric on distributions exactly when k is characteristic. HSIC is the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of the centred cross-covariance. Every result is for a fixed kernel. | Read |
| [NOTE-841](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-841.md) | Tosh, Krishnamurthy & Hsu — contrastive learning, multi-view redundancy and linear models | When two views X and Z are redundant for a label, the predictor that infers Z from X and then predicts, µ(x) = E[E[Y\|Z]\|X=x], is within εX + 2√(εXεZ) + εZ of the Bayes predictor. µ is linear in the density ratio g*(x,·) = p(x,z)/(p(x)p(z)), the optimum of the logistic contrastive problem, so m random landmark evaluations of g* support a linear predictor whose extra error falls as 1/m, scaled by a variance that is at most E[g*²] for bounded labels. Nothing requires the views to be exchangeable. | Read |
| [NOTE-845](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-845.md) | Balestriero, Bottou & LeCun — regularization effects are class dependent | On ImageNet with ResNet-50, making random crop stronger or changing weight decay raises mean test accuracy while some classes lose 20 points or more, and the shift survives a frozen-backbone transfer to iNaturalist. The evidence is per-class curves for hand-picked classes over 10–20 runs, plus a Welch test with no multiple-comparison correction. Theorem 1 says only that a fit to augmentations that are not label-preserving cannot equal the true function. | Read |
| [NOTE-848](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-848.md) | Dwork et al. — The reusable holdout (supplementary material) | From the Supplementary Material: if the max-information between the dataset and the analyst's chosen function is at most log₂e·τ²n, the chance that the function's empirical mean is more than τ above its true mean is at most e^{−τ²n}; pure ε-differential privacy bounds max-information by log₂e·εn. Thresholdout answers m adaptively chosen statistical queries on a holdout of size n = O(ln(m/β)/τ² · min{B, √(B·ln(m/β))/τ}) to accuracy τ with probability 1 − β, where B budgets the times the training estimate is found to overfit. The main text was not read. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-869](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-869.md) | Snell, Lee, Xu & Kumar — Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally | On MATH with PaLM 2-S*, which way of spending test-time compute works best (beam search against a process reward model versus best-of-N; sequential self-revision versus parallel sampling) depends on how hard the question is for the base model, and choosing the method per difficulty bin matches best-of-N with up to about 4× less test-time compute (the discussion says 2–4×). In a FLOPs-matched comparison with a ~14× larger model, the extra test-time compute a small model may spend is set by R, the ratio of total inference tokens to pretraining tokens: when R is small the larger model's pretraining cost buys many samples per query and test-time compute wins on easy and medium questions; when R is large the budget per query falls toward the parameter ratio and the larger model wins, always on the hardest questions. Difficulty estimation (2048 samples per question) and verifier and revision-model finetuning are not counted in the compute, R is an aggregate token ratio with no term for which queries recur, and the evidence is one model family on one benchmark of 500 test questions. | Read |
| [NOTE-873](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-873.md) | Lieder & Griffiths — Resource-rational analysis | Resource rationality defines the right cognitive mechanism as the one, among those a brain can execute, that maximizes expected utility of its result minus the expected opportunity cost of the time and resources it uses (Eq. 3), averaged over the environments consistent with what is known (Eq. 4); resource-rational analysis is a five-step iterate-and-refine method for deriving process models from that objective. The objective is per episode. It has no separate terms for storing a result, retrieving it later, or its going stale: the value of what a computation leaves behind is folded into the utility of the episode's result, and the cost of finding the heuristic in the first place is assigned to evolution and learning and left out. Reuse appears only in the review, qualitatively: habits as reused action sequences, Dasgupta et al. 2018's memorized hypotheses, Howes et al. 2016's memorize-or-look-up trade, and "cognitive prostheses". The framework is offered as a methodological device, not a claim that people are optimal. | Read |
| [NOTE-879](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-879.md) | Hébert-Johnson, Kim, Reingold & Rothblum — Multicalibration: calibration for the computationally-identifiable masses | A predictor is α-multicalibrated on a collection C of subpopulations if, within every set S in C, the individuals given (roughly) the same prediction v have true probabilities averaging within α of v, except on an α-fraction of S. For any C whose sets have size at least γN, a simple iterative patching algorithm reaches multicalibration from O(log\|C\|/α^{11/2}γ^{3/2}) samples in time linear in \|C\|, and the result is a circuit only O(s/α⁴γ) in size when the sets of C are computed by size-s circuits. Learning it is equivalent, up to polynomial factors, to weak agnostic learning of C, so it is hard for rich C under cryptographic assumptions. Calibrating any predictor h on its own level sets as well as on C costs at most 6α in squared error. All guarantees are relative to the benchmark p*, which is itself defined relative to the features available, and they hold only for large sets; the paper offers no uniqueness for the predictor and does not state a theorem in indistinguishability form. | Read |
| [NOTE-881](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-881.md) | Sardana, Portes, Doubov & Frankle — Beyond Chinchilla-optimal: accounting for inference in scaling laws | Fixing a target pre-training loss and adding inference FLOPs (2N per token over a known lifetime demand D_inf) to training FLOPs (6N per token), the compute-minimising model is smaller and trained on more data than Chinchilla-optimal, increasingly so as D_inf approaches and exceeds the training-set size; the optimum has no closed form and is found numerically. The savings are modest in FLOPs (for a 30B-Chinchilla-quality model with 10^13 inference tokens, 28% by training 13.6B on 2.84× the data) and larger in dollars once inference's low hardware utilisation is priced in (17% to 58% in the paper's examples). 47 training runs (150M–6B parameters, 10–10,000 tokens per parameter) find loss still falling at extreme ratios, but more slowly than Chinchilla-fitted laws predict, so the formula overstates the gain from long training. Demand is assumed known before training and fixed given quality; there is no term for uncertainty, discounting, obsolescence or a model being replaced. | Read |
| [NOTE-884](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-884.md) | Jones — Scaling scaling laws with board games | Training AlphaZero on Hex at board sizes 3×3 to 9×9, the best Elo reachable for a given training compute follows one change-point curve across sizes: an incline of about 500 Elo per tenfold of training compute, with the compute for perfect play rising about 7× and the compute to leave random play about 4× per added board row, and fits on small boards predicting larger ones. On 9×9 only, train-time and test-time (tree-search) compute substitute at a fixed rate: at equal Elo, each 10× of train-time compute removes about 15× of test-time compute (fit: log test = −1.2·log train + 0.004·Elo + 29), down to a one-node search, over roughly 1e14–1e16 FLOPS-seconds of training. The trade is an iso-performance curve for a single search; the paper never counts how many games or moves the trained agent will play, so it does not price amortization, and it does not state the unit of test-time compute. One game, small boards, Elo anchored to a perfect player, and no uncertainty on the fitted trade-off coefficients. | Read |
| [NOTE-885](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-885.md) | Dwork, Kim, Reingold, Rothblum & Yona — Outcome Indistinguishability | A predictor p̃ is outcome indistinguishable (OI) relative to a class A of distinguishers when no A ∈ A can tell an individual with Nature's outcome from the same individual with an outcome drawn from Ber(p̃_i). The paper sets out four levels by how much access the distinguisher has to p̃: none, the prediction on the sampled individual, oracle queries, or the code. The lower two levels are equivalent to multi-accuracy and multi-calibration over closely related classes. At those levels OI predictors exist with size O(s/ε²), whatever Nature's complexity. At the oracle level, under fine-grained hardness of clique counting or BPP ≠ PSPACE, some efficient distinguisher classes force any OI predictor to be nearly as expensive as Nature's own predictor. That gives a strict separation between oracle access and sample access. OI never requires p̃ ≈ p*. A predictor is good only relative to A, and with the paper's construction a weak A gives a coarse predictor that a richer A would refute. The paper covers binary outcomes, a fixed representation of individuals and single samples (multi-sample OI is left mostly to future work). | Read |
| [NOTE-981](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-981.md) | Charvin, Catenacci Volpi and Polani — Exact and soft successive refinement of the IB | Defines successive refinement for the information bottleneck as extending a coarse optimum T₁ to a fine optimum (T₁, S), and shows it equivalent to some pair of optima forming X → T₂ → T₁. With an injective fine decoder, it is also equivalent to the coarse decoder points lying in the convex hull of the fine ones, which a linear programme checks. Refinability is proved for binary X and Y, for Y a function of X, and for jointly Gaussian variables. Numerically the hull test on computed optima often fails, and the loss, measured by unique information, stays under a few percent. Those failures are uncertified. Run here with certified optima, the test shows that the four-state source of [CLAIM-387](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-387.md) is not refinable between β = 8 and β = 12: its stochastic optima do not nest either. | Read |
| [NOTE-983](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-983.md) | Rahaman et al. — On the Spectral Bias of Neural Networks | A ReLU network is piecewise linear, so its Fourier transform falls as k^(−d−1) along almost every direction and as k^(−2) along the normals to the faces of its linear regions; that is proved for compactly supported networks only. Trained networks fit low frequencies first, even when high frequencies carry ten times the amplitude, and high-frequency components are the first to be destroyed by parameter noise; both are experiments. The tie from the decay to the order of learning is a heuristic bound, and the volume "proof" in Appendix D does not hold. On a curve embedded in the plane, high latent frequencies are fitted more easily as the curve gets more petals. The paper puts this down to the shape of the curve, but most of it comes from the curve getting longer. | Read |
